Welcome to the new home of WHS Fantasy Football

I've been running this league for over a decade now, so it felt like time we upgraded ourselves — one place to see everything: values, rules, money, and every season we've ever played. This is it. Bookmark it.

For anyone who needs the refresher: this is a fun, easygoing league of high school mates. It's a way to stay in touch all season. The goal is always to have fun — nobody's taking this too seriously. (Well. Almost nobody.)

We're a keeper league. You can hang on to players from last year at a discount, which means drafting well — and hitting on sleepers — pays off for more than just one season. The full system is in The Keeper Rules tab, examples and all.

The money: there's a weekly payout from the pot for the top scorer, so it pays to stay engaged every single week. Whatever's left after the weekly prizes gets split 60% to 1st, 25% to 2nd, 15% to 3rd. The exact numbers are right below.

And no, there's no sacko punishment. You can blame Yi for that, by being the worst sacko commissioner ever. In lieu of suffering, our last-place finishers are enshrined on the Hall of Fame tab's Sacko Wall for permanent mockery. Play to the bitter end, or the wall awaits.

🏈 Open our Yahoo league →

Finding your way around:
Keeper Values — who costs what this year. Find your name, see where you stand, and follow the steps at the bottom to lock your two in on Yahoo.
The Money — the weekly and season-long payouts, and who's currently up.
The Keeper Rules — the whole system, plainly explained, examples included.
League History — every keeper value and every draft, every season we've played.
Hall of Fame — the champions, the Sacko Wall, and the stats that settle arguments (or start new ones).

How to actually set your keepers

Picking them here doesn't count — this page just tells you what everyone costs. You have to enter them in Yahoo yourself, and they're due Saturday, August 15, 2026 at 12:00 AM PDT. It takes about thirty seconds:

  1. Hover “My Team” in the top nav of our league, and pick Keepers from the dropdown that appears.
  2. Tick the checkbox next to the two players you want. Two is the max — one or none is allowed, three is not. Anyone showing a salary of 0 is ineligible this year and can't be kept no matter what; the number beside each name is what he costs you in the draft.
  3. Click “Set Keepers” at the bottom. Nothing is saved until you do. Go back in afterward and check they stuck — you can change your mind as many times as you like right up to the deadline.

Diagrams, not screenshots — Yahoo moves things around every couple of years, but the three steps have stayed put.

The Keeper Rules

Here's the whole system, plain and simple, with real examples so nobody has to guess. Two keepers each, every keeper costs a draft pick. If you spot a note like (rule 8) next to someone's cost, this is the list to check it against.

  1. You can hold onto two players from this year's team when next season rolls around. Zero or one is perfectly fine too, if you'd rather take your chances in the draft — there's just no way to keep a third. Going into 2026, Frank is holding onto Chase Brown and Quinshon Judkins. That's the two he gets — if he wanted a third guy, one of those two would have to go back in the pool.
  2. Whatever round you drafted him in is what he costs you to keep the first time — and every year after that you keep him, the price gets one round cheaper. That discount only builds up in years you actually kept him, though. If you let him go and he ends up back in someone's draft fresh, the clock resets. Take Brock Bowers. Yi took him in the 12th round back in 2024, which round-8-or-later pricing sets at a round 8 to keep. Yi kept him at that price in 2025, and holding onto him again for 2026 drops it down to a round 7 — one cheaper for the second straight keeper year.
  3. A first-round pick can never be a keeper — not that season, not any season after. It's the one rule that trumps everything else on this list, no matter how the rest of a player's value plays out. Bijan Robinson went in round 1 for Anish, and Ashton Jeanty went round 1 for Neil. Doesn't matter how good either one turns out — their cost just reads 0, not eligible.
  4. If a keeper's price would ever decay down to round 1, that's as far as it goes — a round-1 cost isn't allowed, whether he got there by being drafted there (rule 3) or by the discount wearing him down to it. It's the same wall either way, not a different one. In practice, that means a round-2 pick only ever gets kept once: his price only has one round of room to give before it hits that wall. Frank drafted Jahmyr Gibbs in round 2 in 2024 and kept him in 2025 at that same round-2 price. Keeping him again for 2026 would drop his price to round 1 — off limits, exactly like any other first-rounder — so he's back in the draft with a cost of 0, same as Bijan Robinson and Ashton Jeanty up in rule 3. Justin Jefferson, over on Yi's roster, hit the identical wall the identical way.
  5. Three years is the absolute most you can keep the same guy — the season you draft him, plus two keeper years after that. Once those three years are up, he goes back into the draft no matter how cheap he's gotten. Puka Nacua is the clean example. Phil drafted him in round 14 back in 2023, kept him in 2024 for a round-8 price, and kept him again in 2025 at round 7. 2026 would've been his fourth year on Phil's roster and a round-6 price — but the three-year clock had already run out, so he's ineligible and back on the board.
  6. Anyone who lasted until round 8 or later on draft day — or who you scooped up off waivers or free agency during the season — keeps at a flat round-8 price. Doesn't matter if he actually went in round 9 or round 14; round 8 is the floor for everybody down there. Eric drafted Rashee Rice in round 9 in 2025, but he keeps at round 8, not 9. Frank never drafted Quinshon Judkins at all — picked him up mid-season — and he still keeps at that same round 8.
  7. A keeper's price travels with the player, not with whoever's holding him at the moment. Drop him and someone else picks him up, and they inherit exactly the price he already had — it doesn't reset just because he changed hands. Say you're carrying a round-4 keeper and you cut him loose in October. Whoever grabs him off waivers is stuck with that same round-4 price, not a clean round-8 default.
  8. To even be keeper-eligible, he has to have been on your roster for the season's final four weeks and actually played at least one game that year. The cutoff date comes straight from Yahoo's own season calendar, so there's nothing to argue about and nothing anyone can override by hand. 2025 wrapped up December 29, which put the cutoff at December 1. Anish added Michael Carter on December 17 — sixteen days too late — so Carter isn't keeper-eligible. Frank's Courtland Sutton missed it the same way, added that same day.
  9. Your two keepers can't land on the same round. If they do, one of them has to bump up a round, and that becomes his real price from then on — permanently, not just for this year. You pick which one moves; leave it up to chance and ADP breaks the tie for you. Going into 2026, Phil's Matthew Stafford and his Rams D/ST both priced out at round 8. Stafford got bumped up to round 7, so Phil's really spending a 7 and an 8, not two 8s. And that bump sticks around for good — Raj's Jaxon Smith-Njigba got bumped from 8 up to 7 back in 2025, which is exactly why his price is down to round 6 now instead of 7.
  10. On Yahoo's own Choose Keepers page, the salary listed next to each name is his keeper cost — the actual draft round he'll occupy on draft day. A cost of 7 means he takes your round-7 pick. A 0 means he's not eligible this year. Brock Bowers shows a keeper cost of 7. Keep him, and when the draft happens he simply occupies Yi's round-7 pick — Yi picks normally in every other round, but round 7 is already spoken for. Look up Puka Nacua instead and you'd see a 0 — he's not keeper eligible this year, full stop, not just skipped over.
  11. A trade resets a player's three-year keeper clock from rule 5 — but it does not touch his price. Whoever trades for him gets a full fresh three years to work with, starting back at zero used. The cost he already carries comes along exactly as it stood; the years his previous owner already burned off don't transfer with him. Trade for a guy who's already been kept twice under his old owner — meaning rule 5 would've retired him after one more year there — and his new owner still gets a full three years out of him, at whatever discounted price he's already earned. Not a fresh reset back to his original round, just a fresh clock.
  12. Only players still on your roster when the season ends count as keepers. Drop someone in October and never bring him back, and there's simply no keeper value left to talk about — he's just gone. Cut a round-3 keeper in week 8 and that's the end of it for him. Even if you re-add him later that same season, he'd still need to clear rule 8's four-week, actually-played requirement all over again.

Every cost you see on this page comes straight out of these rules, applied in exactly this order — and every number in the examples above is real, pulled right from our own draft history. If a cost ever looks off, the rule that produced it is named right next to it, so you can trace exactly why.
